stemMd: A vaccine leads to a faster and stronger antibody response on later exposure to the same antigen. What accounts for this?

options.label: A
options.textMd: Replacement of the person’s genome with the pathogen’s genome

options.label: D
options.textMd: Permanent conversion of all skin cells into antibodies

options.label: E
options.textMd: A complete halt to innate immunity

explanationMd: Adaptive immune responses generate memory B and T cells specific to encountered antigens. On re-exposure these populations respond more rapidly and effectively than naive cells. Memory is antigen-specific, so vaccination against one pathogen does not imply equal protection against every unrelated pathogen.

distractorRationale.d: Antibodies are molecules, and skin cells are not converted into them.
distractorRationale.b: Removing lymphocytes would impair adaptive immunity.
distractorRationale.a: Immune memory does not require genome replacement.
distractorRationale.e: Vaccination does not work by stopping innate defence.
